newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to cut tax, tighten discipline - minister.
newsitem.headline: Romania to cut tax, tighten discipline - minister.

text.p: Romania plans to strengthen financial discipline and cut taxes to offset recent price hikes triggered by a two-fold increase in fuel prices, Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara said on Thursday.

"We will reduce fiscality and tighten financial discipline," Ciumara told a news conference, his first since he took the finance portfolio in the centrist coalition government formed after last November's general elections.
He said planned changes in fiscal policy involved cuts in income and profit taxes and a more flexible Value Added Tax (VAT) system.
The government doubled fuel prices from January 1 to meet recommendations made by the International Monetary Fund.
Prices for electricity and heating are also expected to rise by the end of January, government sources said recently.

Next week an IMF mission will arrive in Bucharest to start talks on a new loan accord. The Fund last year suspended a $460 million accord on the grounds that the former leftist government failed to meet agreed targets, which also included increases in fuel prices to bring them in line with world levels.
The petrol price increase triggered a chain reaction on a wide range of goods, cutting deeper into the budgets of Romanian consumers with an average monthly wage of about $100.

Ciumara said the planned relaxation in fiscal policy, aimed mainly at cushioning the effects of higher prices on the population, would not drain the state budget of revenues as the new measures would also include steps to fight tax evasion.

Latest data show in the first nine months of 1996 Romanian state-run companies had paid only half of the 4.6 trillion lei worth of wage taxes they owed to the state budget. Wage taxes and VAT account for the bulk of Romania's state revenues.
"I'm confident the new measure will bring in more revenues," Ciumara said.
He did not elaborate on the size of the planned tax cuts but said "many people will benefit from the new eases". The new measures are expected to become effective in March, he said.
Year-on-year inflation last November stood at 47.4 percent, well above a 20 percent target agreed with the IMF.
Local analysts said they expected January inflation to quicken to around 10 percent. But Ciumara declined on Thursday to give an estimate or confirm that figure.
